claims.text: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles comprise five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
Such multimetallic alloys can form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion counteracting a thermodynamic driving force for segregation.
Severe lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys causes low atomic diffusivity.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution phase against intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
Configurational complexity itself imposes kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Sufficiently high kinetic barriers can preserve the solid solution at temperatures as high as 1923 K.
At lower temperatures, reduced atomic motion prevents phase separation.
A critical temperature exists above which diffusion overcomes the kinetic barriers and causes elemental segregation.
Phase stability is determined by the balance between entropic stabilization and diffusion-mediated segregation.
Reactive atmosphere and oxygen chemical potential can affect phase stability.
Reactive conditions can lower diffusion barriers and thereby promote elemental segregation.
Nanoparticles with sufficiently high kinetic barriers will retain a single phase and show minimal chemical redistribution until a critical temperature is reached within 473–1923 K.
The proposed test progressively heats the nanoparticles from 473 K to 1923 K under controlled catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can be used to monitor phase composition and elemental redistribution during heating.
The exact critical temperature and the quantitative effect of catalytic environments on kinetic barriers are unknown.
Segregation or chemical inhomogeneity occurring before the expected critical temperature would falsify the proposed kinetic-stability hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism describe stability as a balance among kinetic barriers, thermodynamic driving forces, configurational entropy, and environment, whereas the falsification rule recasts the hypothesis as claiming that kinetic limitations alone govern stability.
